title: Daily share prices in London and Paris, August 1718 - December 1720 (eight companies)
source: R. G. P. Frehen, W. N. Goetzmann and K. G. Rouwenhorst, 1720 price database ('1720PriceDatabaseOctober5_10version.xlsx', sheet 'British and French shares'), the data of 'New Evidence on the First Financial Bubble', Yale ICF Working Paper 09-04 (2009), published in Journal of Financial Economics 108(3): 585-607 (2013)
series: date (Gregorian calendar, ISO); date_julian (the Julian date used in London, ISO; empty for Paris-only days); prices: bank_of_england, royal_african, old_east_india, south_sea, million_bank, royal_exchange_assurance, london_assurance in pounds per 100 pounds of nominal stock (the two assurance companies' quotations as recorded by the authors), mississippi in livres per share of the Compagnie des Indes (the Mississippi Company); an empty cell is a day without a quotation
license: Each sheet of the workbook reads 'Please do not circulate this data without the expressed permission of the authors'. The .csv is therefore not kept in the repository (it is listed in .gitignore); run data/fetch/fgr2009_1720_shares.py to download the workbook and write it. This .json and the fetch script are kept.
notes: Workbook SHA-256 8c829098d23fd3c8cf11ed0bf61f1d74df86abf68715157c813da0258aee578c. The authors' sources sheet: British shares from Castaing's The Course of the Exchange (British Library copies) and from Larry Neal's data (European State Finance Database); for the Mississippi Company, a series compiled from Velde's database: quotations from the Gazette d'Amsterdam for 6 August 1718 - 5 August 1719, and from Murphy's series for 6 August 1719 - 25 November 1720, completed from the Leydse Courant when Murphy has no quotation or when the official price was fixed (March 1720) while the market price floated. Mississippi prices are in livres of the day: from March 1720 the livre was the Bank's note, whose value in silver fell (Velde 2003, Table 4); the data do not say whether the quotations after the summer of 1720 allow for the conversion of shares at 2 for 3. From 24 June to 22 August 1720 (Julian) the South Sea Company's transfer books were closed and its quotations were for later delivery (Garber 1990, p. 50, n. 11). The highest South Sea price in the data is 950 (29 June - 1 July 1720, Julian), Neal's peak; Scott's 1050 includes a 10 per cent stock dividend. One date is mistyped in the workbook ('20-51719'); the fetch script rebuilds it from the other calendar. 879 days, 6 August 1718 to 31 December 1720 (Gregorian).
citation: Frehen, R. G. P., W. N. Goetzmann and K. G. Rouwenhorst (2013), 'New Evidence on the First Financial Bubble', Journal of Financial Economics 108(3): 585-607; data: Yale ICF 1720 price database
